title: A 15-Year-Old Boy with Primary Maxillary Bone Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase-Positive Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma Relapsed with Rib Metastasis after Spontaneous Remission of a Maxillary Bone Lesion: A Case Report and Literature Review
content:
AbstractAnaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) is a rare form of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) in children, accounting for 10–15% of all NHL cases. ALCL is currently classified as follows: systemic anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)-positive, systemic ALK-negative, primary cutaneous, and breast implant-associated ALCL. In children, systemic ALK-positive ALCL is the most common, and patients often present with extranodal involvement. We report a rare case of systemic ALK-positive ALCL with primary bone involvement in a 15-year-old male patient. Primary bone lymphoma is most commonly observed in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and is extremely rare in systemic ALCL. Therefore, the clinical features and prognosis of primary bone ALCL remain unclear. Our patient had spontaneous remission of primary maxillary bone ALCL after gingival scraping but relapsed 12 months later with rib metastasis. Spontaneous remission of ALCL has been reported frequently in primary cutaneous ALCL and rarely in systemic ALCL. Our case demonstrates for the first time that systemic ALCL can also present as solitary bone involvement that can spontaneously remit. Because systemic ALCL is aggressive and has a risk of relapse, as in our case, it is important to consider ALCL in the differential diagnosis of primary bone lesions and to make a precise pathological diagnosis.

IntroductionAnaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) is a rare form of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) in children, accounting for 10–15% of all NHL cases in the pediatric population [1]. According to the World Health Organization lymphoma classification, there are four types of ALCL: systemic anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)-positive ALCL, systemic ALK-negative ALCL, primary cutaneous ALCL, and breast implant-associated ALCL. In children, 90% of ALCL cases are estimated to be systemic ALK positive [1], and patients frequently present with extranodal involvement, noting that they are often diagnosed at an advanced stage. Systemic ALCL with primary bone lesions presenting as extranodal involvement is very rare [2]. This disease is an aggressive lymphoma, usually treated by multidrug chemotherapy, with only a few reports of spontaneous remission [3–7]. There are no reports of spontaneous remission of primary bone ALCL in systemic ALCL cases. Here, we report a case in which a maxillary lesion showed spontaneous remission after gingival scraping; however, the patient relapsed with rib metastasis 12 months later, leading to a diagnosis of primary bone ALK-positive ALCL. The CARE Checklist has been completed by the authors for this case report, attached as online supplementary material (for all online suppl. material, see www.karger.com/doi/10.1159/000530459).Case PresentationA 15-year-old male patient presented to a community hospital with left-sided chest pain lasting longer than 4 weeks. Chest computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed bone destruction and a dark mass in the left fifth rib. The patient was referred to our hospital for evaluation of the mass. The patient had no family history of cancer at a young age. Approximately 12 months prior to admission, he was diagnosed with buccal cellulitis, maxillary sinusitis, and periapical periodontitis at the root of the left maxillary first molar and second premolar. No apparent originating organism was reported in the bacteriological examination. The patient was subsequently treated with antibiotics for 14 days. However, gingival swelling and fever did not improve. A head CT scan showed a left maxillary lesion with bone destruction (Fig. 1a, left). Intraoperative findings revealed that the buccal bone of the maxillary first and second premolars was deficient, the gingival granulation tissue of the defect was scraped, and no bone removal or drilling was performed. Inflammatory cells were identified in the pathological specimens of the scraped granulation tissue. After the gingival granulation tissue was scraped, the patient recovered from fever, and a second CT scan 8 months after scraping revealed normal findings (Fig. 1a right).Fig. 1.Images at diagnosis of primary and recurrent diseases. a Computed tomography (CT) imaging before scraping surgery at another hospital 12 months before admission showing a maxillary sinus lesion with bone destruction (left). CT 8 months after scraping surgery, which turned normal (right). b Contrast-enhanced MRI on admission to our hospital. The lesion was up to 30 × 30 mm in diameter on the left fifth rib. T2-weighted images were hypointense.On admission, the patient had no fever or lesions in the oral cavity. The left region of his chest was slightly warm but not swollen. No enlarged lymph nodes, hepatosplenomegaly, or rashes were observed. The patient’s serum C-reactive protein was 3.28 mg/dL (normal level, <0.20 mg/dL) and soluble interleukin-2 receptor level was 2,300 U/mL (normal level, 121–613 U/mL). A bone marrow biopsy revealed normocellular marrow without lymphoma cell infiltration. Contrast-enhanced MRI was performed on admission and confirmed the presence of a lesion up to 30 × 30 mm in diameter on the left fifth rib. The tumor was hypointense on both T1- and T2-weighted images (Fig. 1b). Fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography combined with CT showed high fluorodeoxyglucose uptake (maximum standardized value of 26.9) only in the left fifth rib and no uptake in the left maxillary lesion.We reviewed the pathological specimens of the left fifth rib lesion. In the hematoxylin and eosin-stained sections, we detected large atypical cells with densely stained, swollen nuclei, abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, and occasional mitotic figures (Fig. 2a). These tumor cells were immunoreactive for CD30 (Fig. 2b), epithelial membrane antigen, and granzyme B. Their nuclei and cytoplasms were positive for ALK1 immunostaining (Fig. 2b) and negative for CD20 and CD79a. Reexamination of the pathological specimen of the left maxillary bone lesion revealed a sheet-like proliferation pattern of large cells with round, oval, kidney- or horseshoe-shaped nuclei and abundant cytoplasm (Fig. 2c). These tumor cells were positive for CD30 and their nuclei and cytoplasms were positive for ALK1 immunostaining (Fig. 2d). Considering these pathological results, we diagnosed the patient with recurrent systemic ALK-positive ALCL in the left fifth rib, at the primary site of the left maxillary bone. We decided not to surgically remove the lesion on the left fifth rib because the surgery would have been too invasive. Consequently, we followed the ALCL99 standard risk protocol (MTX3 arm) to treat the patient [8]. Although we found that the maxillary bone lesion was also an ALCL, we did not change the treatment because of the absence of high-risk organ involvement. MRI scans were performed several times to evaluate the lesions during treatment. The tumor size decreased from 30 × 30 mm to 16 × 20 mm, and a partial response was observed. A positron emission tomography-CT scan showed no significant accumulation, and a head CT scan revealed no maxillary bone lesions during hospitalization. At the time of writing, the patient has been progression free for 31 months since the completion of treatment.Fig. 2.Histology at diagnosis of primary and recurrent diseases. a Hematoxylin and eosin-stained section of the lesion on the left fifth rib. Atypical large cells with densely stained and swollen nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with occasional mitotic figures were observed. b Immunostained section of the lesion on the left fifth rib. The tumor cells were immunoreactive for CD30, and the nucleus and cytoplasm were positive for ALK1. c Hematoxylin and eosin-stained section of the lesion of the maxillary bone. A sheet-like proliferation pattern of large cells with a round, oval, kidney- or horseshoe-shaped nucleus and abundant cytoplasm wa observed. d Immunostained section of the lesion of the maxillary bone. The tumor cells were positive for CD30 and ALK1 (nuclear and cytoplasmic).DiscussionIn this study, we encountered a case of primary bone ALK-positive ALCL that relapsed with rib metastasis after spontaneous remission without chemotherapy, following a biopsy of a maxillary bone lesion. Spontaneous remission of ALCL has been frequently reported in primary cutaneous ALCL [3] but is rare in systemic ALCL. In Table 1, we summarize 5 reported cases of spontaneous remission of systemic ALCL after biopsy, in addition to our case. The first 2 cases (nos. 1 and 2) mainly had superficial lymph node lesions [3, 4]. The remaining 3 cases (nos. 3, 4, and 5) involved deep lymph nodes, organs, soft tissue, etc. [5–7]. These 5 cases were similar to ours in that the lesions spontaneously remitted after biopsy. In particular, in the 3rd, 4th, and 5th cases, the lesion remained after biopsy but the residual tumor spontaneously remitted, which was similar to our case. All 3 patients evaluated for ALK expression were ALK positive, as was our case. The mechanism of spontaneous remission of lymphoma remains unclear but may be due to changes in the host immune system associated with concurrent infection or biopsy. A traumatic intervention may activate the local immune system through cytotoxic T lymphocytes and therefore remit the lesion [9]. Thus, we cannot underestimate the relationship between biopsy and spontaneous remission. The mechanism behind spontaneous remission of systemic ALCL should therefore be further elucidated.Table 1.Cases with spontaneous remission of systemic ALCL after biopsyPatient numberAge, yearsSexALK expressionPrimary involvementBiopsy methodBiopsy siteTime to relapseRelapse involvementChemotherapy after relapseOutcomeReferences138Male(+)Left axillary lymph nodesExcisional biopsyLeft axillary lymph node(−)(−)Not applicableAlive[3]212Female(+)Right axillary lymph nodesNot mentionedRight axillary lymph node8 yearsLeft inguinal lymph node(+)Alive[4]344MaleNot mentionedLeft inguinal, paraaortic, hilar, and mediastinal lymph nodesBoth lungsStomachLeft supraclavicular regionNot mentionedLeft inguinal lymph nodeLungStomach2 monthsLymph node(+)Alive[5]477MaleNot mentionedLeft-sided soft palateIncisional biopsyLeft-sided soft palate12 monthsLymph node(+)Alive[6]535Female(+)Left axillary lymph nodeSubclavian vesselsThoracic and lumbar spine pelvisIncisional biopsyLeft axillary lymph node(−)(−)Not applicableAlive[7]Our case15Male(+)Maxillary bone (PBL)ScrapingMaxillary bone12 monthsLeft fifth rib bone(+)AlivePBL, primary bone lymphoma; ALK, anaplastic lymphoma kinase.Primary bone lymphoma (PBL) is a very rare subtype that can be defined as a single bone lesion with or without local lymph node involvement. Additionally, it can present as several bone lesions lacking lymph node or visceral involvement [10]. The incidence of PBL is estimated to be approximately 5% of extranodal lymphomas and less than 1% of all NHL cases in adults and children [11]. The most common histological type of PBL is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, whereas primary bone ALCL, the histological type of systemic ALCL as PBL, is extremely rare [10, 12, 13]. The pathogenesis of primary bone ALCL, especially the clinical significance of ALK expression, remains to be elucidated. To our knowledge, no case of spontaneous remission of PBL has been reported in the literature to date; however, our case is valuable in showing that bone lesions in primary bone ALK-positive ALCL can remit spontaneously.Lymphoma, including ALCL, presents with nonspecific symptoms, as lymphadenopathy and fever are common inflammatory diseases that share many of the same features. Particularly in bone lesions, if symptoms improve, a detailed pathological examination for the diagnosis of lymphoma may be omitted because PBL is extremely rare. The prognosis of primary bone ALCL is not yet known; however, ALCL should always be considered since systemic ALCL is generally aggressive and there is a risk of relapse even after spontaneous remission, as in our case. Furthermore, a precise pathological diagnosis is vital in the differential diagnosis of primary bone lesions.AcknowledgmentsWe sincerely thank the patient and his family who contributed to this study.Statement of EthicsWritten informed consent was obtained from the patient and his guardians for publication of this case report and any accompanying images. diagnosis.diagnosis_raw: systemic anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) with primary maxillary bone involvement; relapsed with left fifth rib bone metastasis
diagnosis.disease_name: Systemic ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) with primary bone involvement (maxillary bone) and relapse in left fifth rib
diagnosis.severity_description: aggressive lymphoma; extranodal primary bone involvement; relapse after spontaneous remission
diagnosis.lab_values: CRP 3.28 mg/dL; soluble IL-2 receptor 2,300 U/mL; PET/CT SUVmax 26.9 in left fifth rib
diagnosis.disease_duration_before_healing: Maxillary lesion identified ~12 months before admission; became radiographically normal by 8 months after scraping
diagnosis.cancer_subtype: Systemic ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL); primary bone lymphoma presentation
diagnosis.primary_site: Left maxillary bone (maxillary sinus region; buccal bone near left maxillary first molar/second premolar)

treatment.treatments_raw: Initial antibiotics for presumed infection; gingival granulation tissue scraping (no bone removal/drilling) for maxillary lesion; after relapse treated per ALCL99 standard risk protocol (MTX3 arm) chemotherapy; rib surgery not done due to invasiveness
treatment.surgery_type: Gingival granulation tissue scraping at maxillary lesion (biopsy/traumatic intervention; no bone removal or drilling)
treatment.surgery_outcome: Fever resolved after scraping; CT 8 months later showed normal maxillary findings
treatment.chemotherapy_response: Partial response: rib tumor decreased from 30×30 mm to 16×20 mm; PET/CT showed no significant accumulation; head CT showed no maxillary lesions during hospitalization

remission_outcome.time_to_remission_raw: CT became normal 8 months after gingival scraping of maxillary lesion
remission_outcome.verification_detail: Maxillary lesion with bone destruction on CT improved to normal on CT 8 months after scraping; at relapse, rib lesion seen on CT/MRI and FDG-PET/CT (SUVmax 26.9) with pathology confirming ALK+ ALCL; PET/CT showed uptake only in rib and none in maxilla at relapse evaluation
remission_outcome.tumor_response: Spontaneous radiographic normalization of maxillary lesion after scraping; relapse 12 months later in left fifth rib; after chemotherapy partial response in rib lesion (30×30 mm to 16×20 mm) with PET/CT no significant accumulation
remission_outcome.tumor_size_change: Rib lesion 30×30 mm to 16×20 mm during chemotherapy; maxillary lesion CT abnormal to normal by 8 months post-scraping
remission_outcome.tissue_regeneration_detail: Maxillary bone destruction on CT later appeared normal on CT 8 months after scraping
remission_outcome.follow_up_duration_raw: progression free for 31 months since completion of treatment
remission_outcome.recurrence_timing: 12 months after spontaneous remission of maxillary lesion

validation.statistical_improbability_notes: Systemic ALK+ ALCL is described as aggressive and usually treated with multidrug chemotherapy; spontaneous remission in systemic ALCL is stated to be rare and in this case occurred after scraping/biopsy, followed by relapse at 12 months.
validation.extraction_notes: Age at initial maxillary lesion estimated as ~14 because relapse/admission at 15 occurred ~12 months later. Remission of maxillary lesion is radiographic (CT normalized) after scraping; not clear if complete histologic remission at that time.

analysis.case_summary: A 15-year-old boy had a destructive left maxillary bone lesion that improved to normal on CT 8 months after gingival scraping (initial pathology showed inflammatory cells). Twelve months later he presented with a left fifth rib mass; pathology review of rib and re-reviewed maxillary specimens showed CD30+/ALK1+ systemic ALK-positive ALCL, treated with ALCL99 chemotherapy with partial response and progression-free status 31 months post-treatment.
key_healing_factors: Spontaneous regression of the primary maxillary bone lesion after local traumatic intervention (gingival scraping/biopsy)
Possible immune activation related to biopsy/trauma as discussed by authors
unique_features: Systemic ALK-positive ALCL presenting as solitary primary bone lesion in maxilla with spontaneous remission after scraping
Relapse 12 months later as isolated rib bone metastasis
Spontaneous remission occurred without chemotherapy, temporally associated with biopsy/trauma
analysis.analysis_notes: No psycho-spiritual factors (Turner factors, existential shifts, spiritual practices, anomalous experiences) were reported; the proposed mechanism is biomedical (biopsy/trauma/infection-related immune activation).
